newsitem.title: CHINA: Gore leaves China after discussions with academics.
newsitem.headline: Gore leaves China after discussions with academics.

text.p: U.S. Vice-President Al Gore left Shanghai on Friday at the end of a five-day trip to China which U.S. officials said had helped to improve the often strained relations between the two powers.
Before flying out to Seoul, Gore had a breakfast meeting with 10 Chinese academics to discuss the state of Sino-U.S. relations and political issues in China, U.S. officials said.

Gore's press secretary Ginny Teranzo said the Vice-President met Chinese academics "to discuss the political situation in China", but declined to give any details of the talk or to identify the academics involved.

Gore had two days of tough talks with Chinese leaders in Beijing earlier in the week covering the many sensitive issues which continue to dog relations between the two countries, including human rights, trade and Taiwan.

In a speech on Thursday to American business people in Shanghai, China's financial centre, Gore predicted his two days of talks with Chinese leaders would lead to "significant progress" over the next few months on several issues now dividing Washington and Beijing.
But Gore, the most senior U.S. official to visit China since the crackdown on student demonstrations in Beijing in June 1989, did not specify what areas he expected to see progress in.
"This mission here this week is part of President Clinton's efforts to establish a high-level dialogue that will enable our two nations to build a new era of cooperation for a new century," he said.
"We have had full and vigorous discussions, very productive discussions and I'm optimistic that in the coming months we will make significant progress on many of these issues," he added.
President Clinton in Washington said on Thursday he believed the Gore trip to China had gone well and had validated his administration's policy of engagement with Beijing.
Gore later met with the mayor of Shanghai, Xu Kuangdi, at the city hall and later walked across People's Square in the centre of the city to inspect the new Shanghai Museum.

In his meeting with Gore on Wednesday, Chinese President Jiang Zemin warned the United States not to interfere over Taiwan, hinting the sensitive issue still had the potential to undermine a Sino-U.S. rapprochement.
But Jiang said differences on individual issues should not impair overall ties.

Gore was due to arrive in Seoul for talks with South Korean President Kim Young-sam and a visit to U.S. troops stationed along the Demilitarized Zone that separates the two Koreas. He is scheduled to return to Washington late on Saturday.
